claim: The colon hosts gut microbes that influence glucose homeostasis.
source: The colon hosts gut microbes and glucagon-like peptide 1 secreting cells, both of which influence glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation, drawing from general scientific understanding.

claim: The colon hosts glucagon-like peptide 1 secreting cells that influence glucose homeostasis.
source: The colon hosts gut microbes and glucagon-like peptide 1 secreting cells, both of which influence glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation, drawing from general scientific understanding.

claim: Patients with total colectomy (n = 3,793) had a hazard ratio of clinically recorded type 2 diabetes of 1.40 (95% CI, 1.21 to 1.62; p<0.001) compared with non-colectomy patients.
source: Compared with non-colectomy patients, patients with total colectomy (n = 3,793) had a hazard ratio (HR) of clinically recorded type 2 diabetes of 1.40 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.21 to 1.62; p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Patients with right hemicolectomy (n = 10,989) had a hazard ratio of clinically recorded type 2 diabetes of 1.08 (95% CI, 0.99 to 1.19; p=0.10) compared with non-colectomy patients.
source: Corresponding HRs after right hemicolectomy (n = 10,989), left hemicolectomy (n = 2,513), and sigmoidectomy (n = 13,927) were 1.08 (95% CI, 0.99 to 1.19; p=0.10), 1.41 (95% CI, 1.19 to 1.67; p<0.001) and 1.30 (95% CI, 1.21 to 1.40; p<0.001), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Patients with left hemicolectomy (n = 2,513) had a hazard ratio of clinically recorded type 2 diabetes of 1.41 (95% CI, 1.19 to 1.67; p<0.001) compared with non-colectomy patients.
source: Corresponding HRs after right hemicolectomy (n = 10,989), left hemicolectomy (n = 2,513), and sigmoidectomy (n = 13,927) were 1.08 (95% CI, 0.99 to 1.19; p=0.10), 1.41 (95% CI, 1.19 to 1.67; p<0.001) and 1.30 (95% CI, 1.21 to 1.40; p<0.001), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Patients with sigmoidectomy (n = 13,927) had a hazard ratio of clinically recorded type 2 diabetes of 1.30 (95% CI, 1.21 to 1.40; p<0.001) compared with non-colectomy patients.
source: Corresponding HRs after right hemicolectomy (n = 10,989), left hemicolectomy (n = 2,513), and sigmoidectomy (n = 13,927) were 1.08 (95% CI, 0.99 to 1.19; p=0.10), 1.41 (95% CI, 1.19 to 1.67; p<0.001) and 1.30 (95% CI, 1.21 to 1.40; p<0.001), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The left colon may contribute to maintenance of glucose homeostasis.
source: Although we were not able to adjust for several potential confounders, our findings suggest that the left colon may contribute to maintenance of glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential hazard ratios observed for different types of colectomy in the study.

claim: The gut acts as a key regulator of glucose homeostasis.
source: The gut acts as a key regulator of glucose homeostasis. It influences appetite, gastric emptying, intestinal motility, digestion, and absorption of nutrients, as well as insulin secretion from the pancreas through hormonal secretion and nervous signaling (Holst et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holst et al., 2016.

claim: The gut influences appetite, gastric emptying, intestinal motility, digestion, and absorption of nutrients, as well as insulin secretion from the pancreas through hormonal secretion and nervous signaling.
source: The gut acts as a key regulator of glucose homeostasis. It influences appetite, gastric emptying, intestinal motility, digestion, and absorption of nutrients, as well as insulin secretion from the pancreas through hormonal secretion and nervous signaling (Holst et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holst et al., 2016.

claim: The role of the small intestine in glucose homeostasis has been well elucidated.
source: Whereas the role of the small intestine in glucose homeostasis has been well elucidated (Holst and Madsbad, 2016), the role of the colon is less clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holst and Madsbad, 2016.

claim: The role of the colon in glucose homeostasis is less clear than that of the small intestine.
source: Whereas the role of the small intestine in glucose homeostasis has been well elucidated (Holst and Madsbad, 2016), the role of the colon is less clear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field, contrasting with the well-elucidated role of the small intestine.

claim: The vast majority of gut microbes resides in the colon.
source: The growing interest in the gut microbiota has led to an increased focus on colonic pathophysiology since the vast majority of gut microbes resides in the colon.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge without specific citation.

claim: Patients with type 2 diabetes harbor an altered fecal microbiota.
source: It has been shown that patients with type 2 diabetes harbor an altered fecal microbiota (MetaHIT consortium et al., 2015; Karlsson et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2012), but it is unknown whether it is causally involved in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes (Allin et al., 2015; IMI-DIRECT consortium et al., 2018; MetaHIT Consortium et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to MetaHIT consortium et al., 2015; Karlsson et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2012.

claim: It is unknown whether altered fecal microbiota is causally involved in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes.
source: It has been shown that patients with type 2 diabetes harbor an altered fecal microbiota (MetaHIT consortium et al., 2015; Karlsson et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2012), but it is unknown whether it is causally involved in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes (Allin et al., 2015; IMI-DIRECT consortium et al., 2018; MetaHIT Consortium et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Allin et al., 2015; IMI-DIRECT consortium et al., 2018; MetaHIT Consortium et al., 2016.

claim: Some mechanistic studies in mice suggest that obesity and its related phenotypes can be transmitted via the fecal microbiota.
source: Whereas some mechanistic studies in mice suggest that obesity and its related phenotypes can be transmitted via the fecal microbiota (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Ridaura et al., 2013), elimination of the gut microbiota by antibiotics in humans, does not seem to have any short-term effect on glucose regulation (Mikkelsen et al., 2015; Reijnders et al., 2016; Vrieze et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bäckhed et al., 2004; Ridaura et al., 2013.

claim: Elimination of the gut microbiota by antibiotics in humans does not seem to have any short-term effect on glucose regulation.
source: Whereas some mechanistic studies in mice suggest that obesity and its related phenotypes can be transmitted via the fecal microbiota (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Ridaura et al., 2013), elimination of the gut microbiota by antibiotics in humans, does not seem to have any short-term effect on glucose regulation (Mikkelsen et al., 2015; Reijnders et al., 2016; Vrieze et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mikkelsen et al., 2015; Reijnders et al., 2016; Vrieze et al., 2014.

claim: The colon serves as an endocrine organ.
source: In addition to hosting the gut microbiota, the colon also serves as an endocrine organ.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) secreted by L-cells in the small intestine augments insulin secretion from the pancreatic β-cells in response to a meal.
source: Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) secreted by L-cells in the small intestine augments insulin secretion from the pancreatic β-cells in response to a meal (Holst et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holst et al., 2016.

claim: L-cells are present not only in the small intestine but also in the colon.
source: L-cells are, however, not only present in the small intestine but also in the colon, where the cell density increases from the proximal colon to the rectum (Eissele et al., 1992; Gunawardene et al., 2011; Jorsal et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eissele et al., 1992; Gunawardene et al., 2011; Jorsal et al., 2018.

claim: L-cell density increases from the proximal colon to the rectum.
source: L-cells are, however, not only present in the small intestine but also in the colon, where the cell density increases from the proximal colon to the rectum (Eissele et al., 1992; Gunawardene et al., 2011; Jorsal et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eissele et al., 1992; Gunawardene et al., 2011; Jorsal et al., 2018.

claim: Biologically active GLP-1 is present in colonic tissue in concentrations similar to those in the small intestine.
source: Accordingly, it has been shown that biologically active GLP-1 is present in colonic tissue in concentrations, which are similar to those in the small intestine (Deacon et al., 1995), but the physiological role of colonic GLP-1 remains elusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deacon et al., 1995.

claim: The physiological role of colonic GLP-1 remains elusive.
source: Accordingly, it has been shown that biologically active GLP-1 is present in colonic tissue in concentrations, which are similar to those in the small intestine (Deacon et al., 1995), but the physiological role of colonic GLP-1 remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Colonic L cells secrete the appetite-reducing hormone peptide YY (PYY).
source: In addition to GLP-1, colonic L cells also secrete the appetite-reducing hormone peptide YY (PYY) (Svane et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Svane et al., 2016.

claim: Patients who have undergone resection of the entire colon or parts of it may serve as an opportunity to study the role of the colon in health and disease.
source: Patients who have undergone resection of the entire colon or parts of it, here denoted colectomy, may serve as an evident opportunity to study the role of the colon in health and disease (Jensen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jensen et al., 2015.

claim: Previous studies examining glucose regulation in patients with colectomy suggest that colectomy may influence the entero-insulinar axis, although results are not clear-cut.
source: Glucose regulation in patients with colectomy has been examined in a few previous studies, the largest of which included 21 patients, and although results are not clear-cut, they suggest that colectomy may influence the entero-insulinar axis (Besterman et al., 1982; Nauck et al., 1996; Palnaes Hansen et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Besterman et al., 1982; Nauck et al., 1996; Palnaes Hansen et al., 1997.

claim: Mice raised in the absence of microorganisms have less body fat and are less insulin resistant.
source: On one hand, based on studies showing that mice raised in the absence of microorganisms have less body fat and are less insulin resistant, removal of the human gut microbiota by colectomy may be expected to result in a reduced risk of type 2 diabetes (Bäckhed et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bäckhed et al., 2004.

claim: Removal of the human gut microbiota by colectomy may be expected to result in a reduced risk of type 2 diabetes based on studies in mice raised without microorganisms.
source: On one hand, based on studies showing that mice raised in the absence of microorganisms have less body fat and are less insulin resistant, removal of the human gut microbiota by colectomy may be expected to result in a reduced risk of type 2 diabetes (Bäckhed et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on mouse studies cited (Bäckhed et al., 2004).

claim: Removal of GLP-1 and PYY producing L-cells by colectomy may be expected to lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes.
source: On the other hand, removal of GLP-1 and PYY producing L-cells by colectomy may be expected to lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the known roles of GLP-1 and PYY in glucose homeostasis.

claim: The study identified 8946 individuals with total colectomy in the Danish National Patient Register.
source: We identified 8946 individuals with total colectomy and 90,594 individuals with partial colectomy or proctectomy in the Danish National Patient Register.
evidence: This is a direct report of data extracted from the Danish National Patient Register.

claim: The study identified 90,594 individuals with partial colectomy or proctectomy in the Danish National Patient Register.
source: We identified 8946 individuals with total colectomy and 90,594 individuals with partial colectomy or proctectomy in the Danish National Patient Register.
evidence: This is a direct report of data extracted from the Danish National Patient Register.

claim: The study included 46,279 patients who had undergone total colectomy, partial colectomy, or proctectomy after exclusions.
source: Thus, we included 46,279 patients who had undergone total colectomy, partial colectomy, or proctectomy.
evidence: This is a direct report of the final study population after applying exclusion criteria.

claim: A total of 694,110 age, sex, and year of surgery matched non-colectomy patients who had undergone other types of surgery not involving the gastrointestinal tract were identified for comparison.
source: For comparison, we identified a total of 694,110 age, sex, and year of surgery matched non-colectomy patients who had undergone other types of surgery not involving the gastrointestinal tract (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the control group selection from the study data.

source: Mean (SD) follow-up time was 7.1 (5.2), 5.6 (4.6), 6.3 (4.7), 5.7 (4.8), 6.4 (4.9), 5.8 (4.8) years for patients with total colectomy, right hemicolectomy, resection of the transverse colon, left hemicolectomy, sigmoidectomy, and proctectomy, respectively.

source: Mean (SD) follow-up time was 7.1 (5.2), 5.6 (4.6), 6.3 (4.7), 5.7 (4.8), 6.4 (4.9), 5.8 (4.8) years for patients with total colectomy, right hemicolectomy, resection of the transverse colon, left hemicolectomy, sigmoidectomy, and proctectomy, respectively.

source: Mean (SD) follow-up time was 7.1 (5.2), 5.6 (4.6), 6.3 (4.7), 5.7 (4.8), 6.4 (4.9), 5.8 (4.8) years for patients with total colectomy, right hemicolectomy, resection of the transverse colon, left hemicolectomy, sigmoidectomy, and proctectomy, respectively.

source: Mean (SD) follow-up time was 7.1 (5.2), 5.6 (4.6), 6.3 (4.7), 5.7 (4.8), 6.4 (4.9), 5.8 (4.8) years for patients with total colectomy, right hemicolectomy, resection of the transverse colon, left hemicolectomy, sigmoidectomy, and proctectomy, respectively.

source: Mean (SD) follow-up time was 7.1 (5.2), 5.6 (4.6), 6.3 (4.7), 5.7 (4.8), 6.4 (4.9), 5.8 (4.8) years for patients with total colectomy, right hemicolectomy, resection of the transverse colon, left hemicolectomy, sigmoidectomy, and proctectomy, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of descriptive statistics from the study data.

claim: The cumulative hazard of diabetes was greater among patients who had undergone total colectomy compared with non-colectomy patients.
source: The cumulative hazard of diabetes was greater among patients who had undergone total colectomy compared with non-colectomy patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: Resection of the transverse colon had a hazard ratio of 1.08 (95% CI, 0.76 to 1.54; p=0.66) for diabetes.
source: Resection of the transverse colon was infrequent, but showed the same estimate, although with wider confidence interval; HR 1.08 (95% CI, 0.76 to 1.54; p=0.66), whereas proctectomy was not associated with increased risk of diabetes; HR 0.98 (95% CI, 0.91 to 1.07; p=0.71).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: Proctectomy was not associated with increased risk of diabetes (HR 0.98, 95% CI, 0.91 to 1.07; p=0.71).
source: Resection of the transverse colon was infrequent, but showed the same estimate, although with wider confidence interval; HR 1.08 (95% CI, 0.76 to 1.54; p=0.66), whereas proctectomy was not associated with increased risk of diabetes; HR 0.98 (95% CI, 0.91 to 1.07; p=0.71).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: Total colectomy was associated with increased risk of diabetes in both colorectal cancer patients and patients with other colorectal diseases.
source: In both groups of patients, total colectomy was associated with increased risk of diabetes (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by stratified analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: The HR of diabetes after total colectomy associated with colorectal cancer was 1.61 (95% CI, 1.22 to 2.11, p<0.001).
source: The HR of diabetes after total colectomy associated with colorectal cancer was 1.61 (95% CI, 1.22 to 2.11, p<0.001), whereas the HR for total colectomy associated with other colorectal disease was 1.34 (95% CI, 1.13 to 1.59, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by stratified analysis of the study data.

claim: The HR of diabetes after total colectomy associated with other colorectal disease was 1.34 (95% CI, 1.13 to 1.59, p<0.001).
source: The HR of diabetes after total colectomy associated with colorectal cancer was 1.61 (95% CI, 1.22 to 2.11, p<0.001), whereas the HR for total colectomy associated with other colorectal disease was 1.34 (95% CI, 1.13 to 1.59, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by stratified analysis of the study data.

claim: The HR of diabetes after left hemicolectomy associated with colorectal cancer was 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01 to 1.53, p=0.04).
source: Corresponding HRs were 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01 to 1.53, p=0.04) and 1.88 (95% CI, 1.41 to 2.50, p<0.001) for left hemicolectomy, and 1.11 (95% CI, 0.997 to 1.24, p=0.06) and 1.47 (95% CI, 1.34 to 1.62, p<0.001) for sigmoidectomy.
evidence: This claim is supported by stratified analysis of the study data.

claim: The HR of diabetes after left hemicolectomy associated with other colorectal diseases was 1.88 (95% CI, 1.41 to 2.50, p<0.001).
source: Corresponding HRs were 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01 to 1.53, p=0.04) and 1.88 (95% CI, 1.41 to 2.50, p<0.001) for left hemicolectomy, and 1.11 (95% CI, 0.997 to 1.24, p=0.06) and 1.47 (95% CI, 1.34 to 1.62, p<0.001) for sigmoidectomy.
evidence: This claim is supported by stratified analysis of the study data.

claim: The HR of diabetes after sigmoidectomy associated with colorectal cancer was 1.11 (95% CI, 0.997 to 1.24, p=0.06).
source: Corresponding HRs were 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01 to 1.53, p=0.04) and 1.88 (95% CI, 1.41 to 2.50, p<0.001) for left hemicolectomy, and 1.11 (95% CI, 0.997 to 1.24, p=0.06) and 1.47 (95% CI, 1.34 to 1.62, p<0.001) for sigmoidectomy.
evidence: This claim is supported by stratified analysis of the study data.

claim: The HR of diabetes after sigmoidectomy associated with other colorectal diseases was 1.47 (95% CI, 1.34 to 1.62, p<0.001).
source: Corresponding HRs were 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01 to 1.53, p=0.04) and 1.88 (95% CI, 1.41 to 2.50, p<0.001) for left hemicolectomy, and 1.11 (95% CI, 0.997 to 1.24, p=0.06) and 1.47 (95% CI, 1.34 to 1.62, p<0.001) for sigmoidectomy.
evidence: This claim is supported by stratified analysis of the study data.

claim: When following patients from the date of surgery instead of 1000 days after, the HR of diabetes after total colectomy was 1.72 (95% CI, 1.56 to 1.89).
source: If we, instead of following the patients from 1000 days after surgery, followed the patients from the date of surgery, we found a somewhat higher HR of diabetes after total colectomy: HR = 1.72 (95% CI, 1.56 to 1.89), which, however, should be interpreted with caution due to non-proportional hazards.
evidence: This claim is supported by supplementary analysis of the study data.

claim: HRs of diabetes after left hemicolectomy and sigmoidectomy remained similar to main analyses when follow-up began at the date of surgery.
source: In contrast, HRs of diabetes after left hemicolectomy and sigmoidectomy remained similar to results from the main analyses (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by supplementary analysis of the study data.

claim: When follow-up time began 500 days after surgery or 1500 days after surgery, similar HRs of diabetes were observed as compared to the main analyses.
source: When follow-up time began 500 days after surgery or 1500 days after surgery we observed similar HRs of diabetes as compared to the main analyses (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by supplementary sensitivity analyses of the study data.

claim: The study observed an increased risk of diabetes in colectomy patients.
source: In the present nationwide study, we observed an increased risk of diabetes in colectomy patients.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding supported by the study data.

claim: The risk of diabetes was highest among individuals who had the left part of the colon removed.
source: The risk was highest among individuals who had the left part of the colon removed, whereas resection of the rectum was not associated with any change in risk of diabetes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding supported by the study data.

claim: Resection of the rectum was not associated with any change in risk of diabetes.
source: The risk was highest among individuals who had the left part of the colon removed, whereas resection of the rectum was not associated with any change in risk of diabetes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding supported by the study data.

claim: An increased risk of diabetes was observed irrespective of whether the patients had co-occurring colorectal cancer or other underlying diseases.
source: Moreover, we observed an increased risk of diabetes irrespective of whether the patients had co-occurring colorectal cancer or other underlying diseases.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the stratified analysis findings supported by the study data.

claim: A major strength of the present work is its nationwide nature allowing inclusion of many thousands of patients.
source: A major strength of the present work is its nationwide nature allowing inclusion of many thousands of patients who have had colectomies and a large number of non-colectomy patients leading to relatively narrow confidence intervals of the hazard ratios observed.
evidence: This is a self-assessment of the study design and its implications.

claim: The study did not have information on several potential confounders, precluding adjustment for them.
source: We did not have information on several other potential confounders, precluding adjustment for them.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the study design.

claim: The reported estimates may be positively biased due to inability to adjust for potential confounders.
source: This implies the possibility that the reported estimates may be positively biased.
evidence: This is an inference about potential bias based on the acknowledged limitation.

claim: Colorectal cancer is associated with adiposity.
source: Colorectal cancer is associated with adiposity (Ning et al., 2010), which is also a major risk factor for diabetes, wherefore adiposity may confound our results.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ning et al., 2010.

claim: Adiposity is a major risk factor for diabetes.
source: Colorectal cancer is associated with adiposity (Ning et al., 2010), which is also a major risk factor for diabetes, wherefore adiposity may confound our results.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Adiposity may confound the study results.
source: Colorectal cancer is associated with adiposity (Ning et al., 2010), which is also a major risk factor for diabetes, wherefore adiposity may confound our results.
evidence: This is an inference about potential confounding based on known associations.

claim: If differences in BMI were to fully account for the observed HR of 1.4 of diabetes, a BMI difference of 3 units would be necessary based on previously published data.
source: However, based on previously published data (Berentzen et al., 2011), it can be calculated that if differences in BMI were to fully account for our observed HR of 1.4 of diabetes, a BMI difference of 3 units (equaling a difference of 9 kg for individuals 175 cm tall) would be necessary.
evidence: This is a calculation based on data from Berentzen et al., 2011.

claim: Corticosteroids used for treatment of inflammatory bowel disease have well-documented side-effects resulting in impaired glucose regulation.
source: For example, whereas corticosteroids used for treatment of inflammatory bowel disease have well-documented side-effects resulting in impaired glucose regulation, biologicals such as tumor necrosis factor-α antagonists may alleviate inflammation and therefore potentially improve glucose regulation (Antohe et al., 2012; Parmentier-Decrucq et al., 2009; Solomon et al., 2011; Tam et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Antohe et al., 2012; Parmentier-Decrucq et al., 2009; Solomon et al., 2011; Tam et al., 2007.

claim: Biologicals such as tumor necrosis factor-α antagonists may alleviate inflammation and therefore potentially improve glucose regulation.
source: For example, whereas corticosteroids used for treatment of inflammatory bowel disease have well-documented side-effects resulting in impaired glucose regulation, biologicals such as tumor necrosis factor-α antagonists may alleviate inflammation and therefore potentially improve glucose regulation (Antohe et al., 2012; Parmentier-Decrucq et al., 2009; Solomon et al., 2011; Tam et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Antohe et al., 2012; Parmentier-Decrucq et al., 2009; Solomon et al., 2011; Tam et al., 2007.

claim: It seems unlikely that the findings are due to differences in medication given the ambiguous effects of medication on glucose regulation and the enhanced risk observed in both cancer and non-cancer patients.
source: As the effects of medication on glucose regulation are ambiguous, and since we observed an enhanced risk of diabetes among patients with colorectal cancer and other colorectal diseases, it seems unlikely that our findings are due to differences in medication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results across different patient groups.

claim: The underlying disease may directly increase the risk of diabetes either through its effect on normal colonic function or via other pathways.
source: Also, confounding by indication, that is, the indication for the colectomy — in this case the underlying disease — may bias our results. Hence, the underlying disease may, either through its effect on the normal colonic function or via other pathways, directly increase the risk of diabetes.
evidence: This is speculation about potential confounding by indication.

claim: The fact that similar results were achieved when starting follow-up 1000 days or 1500 days after surgery may speak against confounding by indication.
source: Likely, the fact that we achieved similar results when we started the follow-up time 1000 days after the surgery in our main analyses or 1500 days after surgery in the supplemental analyses may speak against such confounding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of results across different follow-up start times.

claim: Differences in lifestyle factors such as physical activity, smoking, dietary habits, alcohol and coffee drinking may have played a role as confounders.
source: Last, differences in the life style,for example in physical activity, smoking, dietary habits, including alcohol and coffee drinking, of the colectomy versus the non-colectomy groups may have played a role as confounders.
evidence: This is speculation about potential unmeasured confounding.

claim: Patients with undiagnosed diabetes and with diabetes diagnosed outside hospitals but not recorded later in hospitals were missed, and the observed incidence is an underestimation.
source: This implies that patients with undiagnosed diabetes and with diabetes diagnosed outside hospitals, but not recorded later in the hospitals, were missed, and that the observed incidence is an underestimation.
evidence: This is an inference about potential misclassification based on the data source limitations.

claim: The likelihoods of being referred to a hospital or an outpatient clinic and thus the likelihoods of being registered with a clinical diagnosis of diabetes are presumed to be the same in colectomy and non-colectomy patients.
source: However, as we defined the non-colectomy group as individuals who had undergone various other types of surgery, we presume that the likelihoods of being referred to a hospital or an outpatient clinic, and thus the likelihoods of being registered with a clinical diagnosis of diabetes, are the same in the colectomy and non-colectomy patients.
evidence: This is an assumption made about the comparability of the study groups.

claim: The outcome diabetes based on diagnosis code E14 (unspecified diabetes) may be subject to misclassification regarding the type of diabetes.
source: Further, the outcome diabetes based on the diagnosis code E14 (unspecified diabetes) may be subject to misclassification regarding the type of diabetes.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of potential misclassification in the outcome measure.

claim: The study population was restricted to individuals above 30 years to avoid misclassification of type 2 diabetes as type 1 diabetes.
source: The data available does not allow validation of the recorded diagnosis, but to avoid misclassification of type 2 diabetes as type 1 diabetes, we restricted the study population to individuals above 30 years, since type 1 diabetes is much more frequently diagnosed before than after that age.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological decision to reduce misclassification.

claim: Type 1 diabetes is much more frequently diagnosed before than after age 30.
source: The data available does not allow validation of the recorded diagnosis, but to avoid misclassification of type 2 diabetes as type 1 diabetes, we restricted the study population to individuals above 30 years, since type 1 diabetes is much more frequently diagnosed before than after that age.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Type 1 diabetes is infrequent compared to type 2 diabetes, reducing the risk of significant misclassification.
source: Also, type 1 diabetes is infrequent compared to type 2 diabetes, reducing the risk of significant misclassification in this regard (Diabetesforeningen, 2018 Facts about diabetes in Denmark https://diabetes.dk/diabetesforeningen/in-english/facts-about-diabetes-in-denmark.aspx).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Diabetesforeningen, 2018.

claim: The prospective design, including a 1000 days delay after surgery, supports causality since the outcome occurred after the exposure.
source: Indeed, our prospective design, including a 1000 days delay after surgery, supports causality since the outcome occurred after the exposure and the risk remained equally elevated throughout the follow-up periods.
evidence: This is an inference about causality based on the temporal relationship in the study design.

claim: The risk of diabetes remained equally elevated throughout the follow-up periods.
source: Indeed, our prospective design, including a 1000 days delay after surgery, supports causality since the outcome occurred after the exposure and the risk remained equally elevated throughout the follow-up periods.
evidence: This is a description of the pattern observed in the study data.

claim: The finding of increased risk following only colectomy including the left part of the colon, but not the remainder part or the rectum, suggests a specific causal effect of that part rather than a general effect of surgery on the colon.
source: The finding of increased risk following only colectomy including the left part of the colon, but not the remainder part or the rectum, suggests a specific causal effect of that part rather than a general effect of surgery on the colon, which would more likely reflect confounding.
evidence: This is an inference about causality based on the specificity of the association.

claim: Experimental proof of a direct causal effect of colectomy on diabetes risk in humans is impossible.
source: Obviously, experimental proof of a direct causal effect of colectomy on diabetes risk in humans is impossible, and epidemiological substitutes, such as instrumental variable analyses, for example by Mendelian randomization, may not be feasible.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of establishing causality in human studies.

claim: The findings may be explained by removal of GLP-1 producing cells.
source: Thus, it may be speculated that our findings are explained by removal of GLP-1 producing cells or alterations of the colonic gut microbiota composition and function.
evidence: This is speculation about potential biological mechanisms.

claim: The findings may be explained by alterations of the colonic gut microbiota composition and function.
source: Thus, it may be speculated that our findings are explained by removal of GLP-1 producing cells or alterations of the colonic gut microbiota composition and function.
evidence: This is speculation about potential biological mechanisms.

claim: Recent studies suggest that modifications in GLP-1 release are directly involved in both development of diabetes and diabetes remission after gastric bypass.
source: Recent studies suggest that modifications in GLP-1 release are directly involved in both development of diabetes (Færch et al., 2015) and diabetes remission after gastric bypass (Holst and Madsbad, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Færch et al., 2015 and Holst and Madsbad, 2016.

claim: The L-cell density increases from the proximal to the distal colon.
source: Interestingly, the L-cell density increases from the proximal to the distal colon (Eissele et al., 1992; Gunawardene et al., 2011), and accordingly, we observed the highest risk among individuals who had the left part of the colon removed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eissele et al., 1992; Gunawardene et al., 2011.

claim: The highest risk of diabetes was observed among individuals who had the left part of the colon removed, which is consistent with the L-cell density gradient.
source: Interestingly, the L-cell density increases from the proximal to the distal colon (Eissele et al., 1992; Gunawardene et al., 2011), and accordingly, we observed the highest risk among individuals who had the left part of the colon removed.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the L-cell density gradient with the observed risk pattern.

claim: The bacterial load increases along the length of the colon.
source: The bacterial load also increases along the length of the colon (Donaldson et al., 2016), and colectomies involving the left part of the colon therefore likely lead to removal of a larger part of the colonic microbiota than colectomies involving the right part of the colon.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Donaldson et al., 2016.

claim: Colectomies involving the left part of the colon likely lead to removal of a larger part of the colonic microbiota than colectomies involving the right part of the colon.
source: The bacterial load also increases along the length of the colon (Donaldson et al., 2016), and colectomies involving the left part of the colon therefore likely lead to removal of a larger part of the colonic microbiota than colectomies involving the right part of the colon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the bacterial load gradient cited from Donaldson et al., 2016.

claim: Ileocolonic resection leads to an altered colonization of the neo-terminal ileum.
source: Notably however, it has been shown that ileocolonic resection leads to an altered colonization of the neo-terminal ileum (GETAID et al., 2016) suggesting that removal of the colonic gut microbiota may be somewhat compensated for by over-colonization of the remaining parts of the gastrointestinal tract.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to GETAID et al., 2016.

claim: Removal of the colonic gut microbiota may be somewhat compensated for by over-colonization of the remaining parts of the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Notably however, it has been shown that ileocolonic resection leads to an altered colonization of the neo-terminal ileum (GETAID et al., 2016) suggesting that removal of the colonic gut microbiota may be somewhat compensated for by over-colonization of the remaining parts of the gastrointestinal tract.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding cited from GETAID et al., 2016.

claim: Bacterial overgrowth may change the microbiota-mediated conversion of primary bile acids to secondary bile acids, which through their hormone-like actions impact glucose metabolism.
source: Such bacterial overgrowth may well change the microbiota-mediated conversion of primary bile acids to secondary bile acids, which through their hormone-like actions impact glucose metabolism (Ridlon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism, with citation to Ridlon et al., 2014 for the role of bile acids.

claim: Proctectomy was not associated with an increased risk of diabetes with quite narrow upper confidence limits.
source: In our study, proctectomy was, with quite narrow upper confidence limits, not associated with an increased risk of diabetes.
evidence: This is a summary of the study finding for proctectomy.

claim: Feces and bacteria are only present in the rectum during short time periods preceding defecation, hindering continuous signaling between the lumen of the rectum and extra-intestinal tissues.
source: This may be explained by the fact that feces, and thus bacteria and other stimuli of L-cells, is only present in the rectum during the short time periods preceding defecation, thus hindering continuous signaling between the lumen of the rectum and extra-intestinal tissues.
evidence: This is speculation about why proctectomy was not associated with increased diabetes risk.

claim: Removal of the entire colon or a part of it might influence the exchanges between the gut epithelium and ingested food and fluids, especially due to altered bacterial degradation of indigestible fibers to short-chain fatty acids.
source: Last, the removal of the entire colon or a part of it might influence the exchanges between the gut epithelium and ingested food and fluids, especially due to an altered bacterial degradation of otherwise indigestible fibers to short-chain fatty acids, which could in turn have an impact upon diabetes development (Allin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism, with citation to Allin et al., 2015.

claim: The largest previous study examining glucose regulation in colectomy patients included 10 patients with an ileo-anal reservoir and 11 patients with an ileostomy who underwent an oral glucose tolerance test.
source: Among the previous studies that have examined glucose regulation in colectomy patients (Besterman et al., 1982; Nauck et al., 1996; Palnaes Hansen et al., 1997), the largest included 10 patients with an ileo-anal reservoir and 11 patients with an ileostomy who underwent an oral glucose tolerance test (Palnaes Hansen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a description of previous research with citations.

claim: Compared with healthy controls, colectomy individuals had higher peak levels of plasma glucose and higher peak levels and area under the curve of plasma insulin suggesting impaired glucose tolerance and hyperinsulinemia.
source: Compared with 10 healthy individuals, colectomy individuals had higher peak levels of plasma glucose and higher peak levels and area under the curve of plasma insulin suggesting impaired glucose tolerance and hyperinsulinemia.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a previous study (Palnaes Hansen et al., 1997).

claim: The healthy controls in the previous study had lower body weight compared with the colectomy patients.
source: However, the healthy controls had lower body weight compared with the patients, and no major differences in plasma GLP-1 levels were observed (Palnaes Hansen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a description of a limitation in a previous study (Palnaes Hansen et al., 1997).

claim: No major differences in plasma GLP-1 levels were observed between colectomy patients and healthy controls in the previous study.
source: However, the healthy controls had lower body weight compared with the patients, and no major differences in plasma GLP-1 levels were observed (Palnaes Hansen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a description of findings from a previous study (Palnaes Hansen et al., 1997).

claim: The prior evidence from previous studies for an association between colectomy and impaired glucose regulation is conflicting.
source: The prior evidence from these studies for an association between colectomy and impaired glucose regulation is thus conflicting.
evidence: This is a summary assessment of previous literature.

claim: In a previous study based on the Danish National Patient Register, no corresponding difference in cardiovascular disease risk was found between individuals who had undergone total colectomy and individuals who had undergone other types of surgeries leaving the gastrointestinal tract intact.
source: In a previous study also based on the Danish National Patient Register, we found no corresponding difference in cardiovascular disease risk between individuals who had undergone a total colectomy and individuals who had undergone other types of surgeries leaving the gastrointestinal tract intact (Jensen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jensen et al., 2015.

claim: An increased risk of diabetes would be expected to associate with subsequent increased risk of cardiovascular diseases.
source: While we would expect that an increased risk of diabetes would associate with subsequent increased risk of cardiovascular diseases, this discrepancy may be explained by the limited follow-up time, not allowing presence of diabetes yet to be manifested in increased cardiovascular risk.
evidence: This is stated as an expectation based on established knowledge.

claim: The discrepancy between increased diabetes risk and no increased cardiovascular disease risk may be explained by limited follow-up time.
source: While we would expect that an increased risk of diabetes would associate with subsequent increased risk of cardiovascular diseases, this discrepancy may be explained by the limited follow-up time, not allowing presence of diabetes yet to be manifested in increased cardiovascular risk.
evidence: This is speculation about why the findings differ from expectations.

claim: Clinical-physiological studies are warranted to establish whether colectomy per se is associated with metabolic alterations indicating an increased risk of type 2 diabetes.
source: As our findings are based solely on register data, clinical-physiological studies are warranted to establish whether colectomy per se is associated with metabolic alterations indicating an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, and to understand the role of the colon in glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the study limitations.

claim: The Danish National Patient Register covers hospital inpatient and outpatient contacts for Danish patients from 1994 and onwards.
source: The study is based on data from the Danish National Patient Register, which covers hospital inpatient and outpatient contacts for Danish patients from 1994 and onwards (Lynge et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the data source with citation to Lynge et al., 2011.

claim: Non-colectomy patients were selected from three groups: patients who had undergone orthopedic surgery, patients who had undergone abdominal surgery leaving the gastrointestinal tract intact, and patients who had undergone other surgery unrelated to the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Thus, the non-colectomy patients were selected from three groups of patients, and we selected five non-colectomy patients per colectomy patient from each group: (1) patients who had undergone orthopedic surgery, (2) patients who had undergone abdominal surgery leaving the gastrointestinal tract intact, and (3) patients who had undergone other surgery, unrelated to the gastrointestinal tract (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: Non-colectomy patients were matched to colectomy patients by sex, year of birth (±1 year), and date of surgery (±1 year).
source: Non-colectomy patients were matched to colectomy patients by sex, year of birth (±1 year), and date of surgery (±1 year).
evidence: This is a description of the matching procedure in the study design.

claim: Random sampling with replacement was used for selecting non-colectomy patients, meaning individual non-colectomy patients may have been selected more than once.
source: The same series of matching patients may have been used for selection or non-colectomy patients for more than one colectomy patient implying that the individual non-colectomy patient may have been selected more than once (random sampling with replacement).
evidence: This is a description of the sampling method used in the study design.

claim: Clinically recorded type 2 diabetes was defined as ICD-10 codes E11 and E14.
source: The outcome, clinically recorded type 2 diabetes, was defined as the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Edition (ICD-10) codes E11 and E14.
evidence: This is a description of the outcome definition in the study.

claim: Individuals who had a diagnosis of diabetes recorded before surgery were excluded.
source: Individuals who had a diagnosis of diabetes recorded before surgery were excluded.
evidence: This is a description of an exclusion criterion in the study design.

claim: The main analyses were based on those who were alive and who did not have a diagnosis of diabetes recorded during the first 1000 days after surgery.
source: We based our main analyses on those who were alive and who did not have a diagnosis of diabetes recorded during the first 1000 days after the surgery, for two reasons.
evidence: This is a description of the analytical approach in the study design.

claim: Colectomy patients had an increased hazard rate of death after surgery, which may reflect postsurgical morbidity possibly influencing diabetes risk.
source: First, as expected, colectomy patients had an increased hazard rate of death after surgery, which may reflect postsurgical morbidity possibly influencing diabetes risk for other reasons than effects of colectomy as such; the mortality among patients with total colectomy decreased during this period and stabilized from about 1000 days after surgery (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a description of an observed pattern in the data that informed the analytical approach.

claim: The mortality among patients with total colectomy decreased and stabilized from about 1000 days after surgery.
source: First, as expected, colectomy patients had an increased hazard rate of death after surgery, which may reflect postsurgical morbidity possibly influencing diabetes risk for other reasons than effects of colectomy as such; the mortality among patients with total colectomy decreased during this period and stabilized from about 1000 days after surgery (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a description of an observed pattern in the data.

claim: Diabetes may be associated with the diseases leading to colectomy and may still be undiagnosed or not recorded at the time of surgery but possibly recorded during the first years following surgery.
source: Second, diabetes may be associated with the diseases leading to colectomy, and may still be undiagnosed or not recorded at the time of surgery, but possibly so during the first years following surgery.
evidence: This is reasoning about potential reverse causation that informed the analytical approach.

claim: The follow-up time for each participant ended at occurrence of diabetes, death, or at the end of the study (December 18th 2015), whichever came first.
source: The follow-up time for each participant ended at occurrence of diabetes, death, or at the end of the study, December 18th 2015, whichever came first, and the underlying time scale was time from 1000 days after surgery.
evidence: This is a description of the follow-up procedure in the study design.

claim: None of the participants were lost during follow-up.
source: None of the participants were lost during follow-up.
evidence: This is a statement about the completeness of follow-up in the study.

claim: Cox regression models included adjustment for the matching variables: sex, age and year of surgery.
source: To optimize the efficiency and minimize bias (Sjölander and Greenland, 2013) of the comparisons of the colectomy and non-colectomy patients, the Cox regression models included adjustment for the matching variables, sex, age and year of surgery.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis approach with citation to Sjölander and Greenland, 2013.

claim: Separate Cox regression models were fitted for total colectomy and for each type of partial colectomy and proctectomy and their respective non-colectomy patients.
source: Separate models were fitted for total colectomy and for each type of partial colectomy and proctectomy and their respective non-colectomy patients.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis approach.

claim: The study population was stratified into a group including patients with co-occurrence of colorectal cancer at the date of colectomy and a group including the remaining patients.
source: To elucidate whether the underlying disease, for which the colectomy was performed, influenced the subsequent risk of diabetes, the study population was stratified into two groups: a group including patients with co-occurrence of colorectal cancer (ICD-10 codes C18-C20) at the date of colectomy and a group including the remaining patients (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of a stratified analysis approach.
